claims.text: Adding approximately 1–2 wt.% molybdenum to carbon or low-alloy steel promotes formation of Mo-rich sub-oxides.
Adding approximately 1–2 wt.% molybdenum promotes localized chromium segregation at grain boundaries.
Mo-rich sub-oxides and grain-boundary chromium segregation enhance the kinetics of passive-film formation.
Mo-rich sub-oxides and grain-boundary chromium segregation improve the uniformity of the passive film.
The resulting passive-film changes improve corrosion resistance in saline environments.
Molybdenum accelerates chromium segregation to corrosion-critical microstructural locations.
Molybdenum aids formation of secondary Mo-rich oxide phases.
A more homogeneous and protective passive film slows pitting initiation.
A more homogeneous and protective passive film slows localized-corrosion propagation.
Mo-doped samples will exhibit higher pitting potentials than otherwise identical Mo-free samples.
Mo-doped samples will exhibit lower corrosion current densities than otherwise identical Mo-free samples.
Mo-doped samples will form a more uniform and robust passive film than Mo-free samples.
Mo-rich oxide regions and chromium segregation will spatially correlate with areas of enhanced corrosion resistance.
The proposed comparison uses identically processed Mo-free and approximately 1–2 wt.% Mo steels tested in 3.5 wt.% NaCl at room temperature.
Potentiodynamic polarization, impedance spectroscopy, TEM, and EDS mapping will be used to connect corrosion metrics with the proposed microstructural mediators.
The hypothesis is expected to apply under moderate saline exposure at room temperature.
Applicability to high temperatures, more aggressive media, or different alloy systems is uncertain.
